fuller.text: This is a short essay by Paul Graham asking why talk about politics and religion turns out so uniquely useless. He starts from an everyday observation: on online forums, any mention of religion tends to slide into a religious argument. That does not happen with topics like Javascript, a programming language, or baking, so he asks what makes the difference.

That does not happen with topics like Javascript, a programming language, or baking, so he asks what makes the difference.

fuller.text: Graham says the answer matters for more than forum manners. If his theory is right, it tells us not just which discussions to avoid, but how to have better ideas.

fuller.text: His first clue is that people feel no need for any expertise before giving opinions on religion. Strong beliefs are enough, and anyone can have those, so religion threads grow faster than technical ones. Politics works the same way: there is no threshold of expertise, meaning no level of knowledge people feel they must reach first.

Politics works the same way: there is no threshold of expertise, meaning no level of knowledge people feel they must reach first.

fuller.text: He then tests one possible explanation and rejects it. Perhaps these topics have no definite answers, so nobody can be proven wrong and every opinion seems equally valid. But some political questions do have definite answers, such as what a new policy will cost, and those precise questions go just as badly.

Perhaps these topics have no definite answers, so nobody can be proven wrong and every opinion seems equally valid.
But some political questions do have definite answers, such as what a new policy will cost, and those precise questions go just as badly.

fuller.text: His own answer is that religion and politics become part of people's identity, their sense of who they are. People can never argue usefully about something that is part of their identity, because they are bound to take a side. Which topics touch identity depends on the people, not the topic. A battle involving the listeners' own countries would likely spark a political fight, while a Bronze Age battle probably would not, since no one would know which side to take.

fuller.text: From this idea, Graham draws several further points. A question that sparks "religious wars" is not therefore unanswerable; programming languages can be better or worse designed, even though programmers identify with them. You can discuss such questions usefully if you leave out people who respond from identity. Harmless-seeming topics, like Ford versus Chevy pickup trucks, can be unsafe with some people, while politics could in principle be discussed well with others. In a note he adds that the slide happens fast, as more people join and their angry posts draw angrier replies.

fuller.text: He admits a possible exception: some things may be worth including in your identity, such as being a scientist. He argues this label commits you to no particular belief, only to following the evidence wherever it leads. It is like a cupboard sign saying it must stay empty: something is technically inside, but not in the ordinary sense.

fuller.text: The conclusion follows from the theory: if people cannot think clearly about what is part of their identity, let as few things in as possible. Graham says this goes beyond tolerance, where you call yourself one thing but accept others. The step further is not to call yourself that thing at all, because the more labels you have, the dumber they make you.

brief.text: This short essay by Paul Graham asks why arguments about politics and religion go nowhere. His answer is that these topics become part of people's identity, meaning who they feel they are. People can't argue usefully about something that is part of who they are. So the trouble comes from identity, not from the topic itself.
